Foundations: How UX Design Works

Learn what UX design really is, the five components of usability, and the design thinking process professionals use. Set up a low-cost toolkit, choose a practice project, and learn to run research ethically.
What UX design is and the problems it solves
Define user experience (UX) and explain how it differs from user interface (UI) design
Name the five quality components of usability: learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors and satisfaction

**User experience (UX)** is everything a person feels and does while using a product: finding it, learning it, getting a task done, recovering from a mistake, and deciding whether to come back. A **UX designer** studies real users, finds where they struggle, and shapes the product so the task becomes easy, quick and safe. The product can be a mobile app, a website, a USSD menu, or even a paper form at a bank.

**User interface (UI)** is the part you can see and touch: buttons, colours, fonts, icons, screens. UI is one part of UX. A beautiful screen can still give a bad experience if the button you need is hidden, the words are confusing, or the app forgets what you typed when the network drops. In this course you will spend most of your time on the thinking that comes before colours: understanding people, organising content, sketching layouts and testing them.

Usability: the measurable core of UX
Jakob Nielsen of the Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) describes **usability** with five quality components. You will use these words for the rest of the course, so learn them well:

Can a new user send money on a wallet app on day one without help?

Does buying airtime take 4 taps or 12?

Usability is about whether people **can** use a product. **Utility** is whether the product does something they **need**. NN/g puts it simply: useful means usable plus has utility. An app that looks easy but does not let a market woman record credit sales has no utility for her.
Problems UX design solves
**Drop-off:** people start signing up, then give up at a long or confusing form.
**Costly mistakes:** a transfer goes to the wrong account because the app did not show the account name before confirming.
**Support overload:** staff answer the same WhatsApp questions every day because the app does not explain itself.
**Lost trust:** a payment screen spins with no message, so the user does not know if her money left her account and pays twice.
**Exclusion:** small text, low contrast or English-only wording shuts out older users, people with poor eyesight or users with less schooling.
Worked example: the transfer that went quiet

For example, Amaka in Onitsha sends 25,000 naira (approximate) to her supplier using a mobile banking app. After she enters her PIN, the screen shows a spinning circle for about 40 seconds on a weak network, then returns to the home screen with no message.
Amaka does not know whether the money left. She checks her balance, but the debit has not shown yet.
She tries again. Both transfers eventually go through, so she has sent 50,000 naira instead of 25,000.
A UX designer studying this would name the problem: poor **visibility of system status** and no protection against a **duplicate transaction**.
Possible design fixes: show a clear 'Processing, do not retry' message, a transaction reference, and a warning if the same amount is sent to the same account within a few minutes.
The fix is not a new colour. It is clear feedback at the right moment and a guard against a likely error. That is UX work: it reduces losses, support calls and fear.
Why UX matters for trust

People judge an app quickly. When a fintech, school or health app feels confusing, many users assume it is unsafe. Clear wording, honest status messages, predictable buttons and easy ways to undo mistakes all signal that the organisation respects its users. For the WODDI community, good UX can mean the difference between a mother finishing an online course and giving up because she could not find her certificate.

The Double Diamond

The UK Design Council describes a similar process called the **Double Diamond**. The first diamond is about the problem: **Discover** (go wide, research) then **Define** (narrow to the real problem). The second diamond is about the solution: **Develop** (go wide, many ideas) then **Deliver** (narrow to one, test and launch). The shape reminds you to open up before you close down, twice. Many teams fail by jumping straight to a solution before they understand the problem.

Core vocabulary
**User research:** methods for learning about users, such as interviews, observation, surveys and testing.
**Pain point:** a specific moment of frustration, delay, cost or fear in a user's task. Example: 'I cannot find my receipt after paying school fees.'
**Persona:** a short, realistic profile of a type of user, built from research, not imagination. It includes goals, frustrations, devices and context.
**Journey map:** a timeline of the steps a user takes to reach a goal, with what she does, thinks and feels at each step.
**Information architecture (IA):** how content is organised, grouped and labelled so people can find things.
**User flow:** the path of screens and decisions a user goes through to finish one task.
**Wireframe:** a simple black-and-white layout of a screen showing structure, not colours.
**Prototype:** a version of the design people can click or tap through to test the flow.
**Usability test:** watching real users try to complete tasks with your design while you note where they struggle.
**Heuristic evaluation:** an expert review of a design against recognised rules of thumb, such as Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics.
**Accessibility:** designing so people with disabilities, including poor eyesight, hearing loss or limited hand movement, can use the product.
Worked example: from pain point to 'How might we'
For example, Funke volunteers for a women's learning network. Members keep sending WhatsApp messages asking where to download their course certificates.
Empathise: Funke speaks with 6 members by phone. Four of them say they looked under 'Profile' first; two gave up after 5 minutes.
Define: she writes a problem statement: 'Members who finish a course cannot find their certificate because it sits under Settings, which they do not associate with achievements.'
She turns it into a question: 'How might we help members find their certificate in under 30 seconds right after finishing?'
Ideate: she lists 8 ideas, including a 'Download certificate' button on the course completion screen and a 'My certificates' item in the main menu.
Prototype and test: she sketches two options on paper and shows them to 5 members, timing how long each takes to find the certificate.
The 'How might we' question keeps the team focused on the user's goal and gives a clear target (under 30 seconds) to test against.
Write problem statements about users, not features
A weak statement says 'We need a new menu.' A strong one says who struggles, with what task, and why: 'First-time users cannot find X because Y.' The solution comes later.

Research ethics: consent first

When you interview or test with people, you are collecting personal information. Treat it with care. Always get **informed consent**: the person understands what you are doing, why, how long it takes, what you will record, and that they can stop at any time without any penalty. Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), sets rules for processing personal data, including having a lawful basis such as consent and keeping data secure. You are not a lawyer, but you should follow the basic principles: collect only what you need, keep it safe, and delete it when you are done.
Worked example: a 60-second consent script
For example, Zainab is about to interview a tailor in Kaduna about how customers book fittings.
She says: 'Thank you for helping. I am learning UX design and studying how customers book fittings. It will take about 20 minutes.'
'There are no right or wrong answers. I am testing ideas, not testing you.'
'May I record our voices so I do not miss anything? Only I will listen, and I will delete it after writing notes. I will not use your name in my report.'
'You can skip any question or stop at any time.'
She waits for a clear 'yes', notes the date and that consent was given, and only then starts the recording.
The participant feels respected and relaxed, and Zainab has a clear record that consent was given before recording began.

Protect people and yourself

Never ask for bank PINs, passwords, BVN or account numbers during research, even in a test prototype. Use fake data such as 'Account: 0123456789'. Meet participants in public or familiar places, or by phone, and tell someone where you are going.
Recruiting the right people

Your participants should match the people who will really use the product. If your project is a booking flow for a salon, talk to the salon's customers, not your designer friends. Aim for a mix: some confident smartphone users and some who find apps harder, different ages, and, if relevant, people who prefer Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo or Yoruba. A short screening question such as 'How did you last book an appointment?' helps you choose people with real experience of the task. Thank participants for their time; a small token such as airtime is common, but say clearly that it does not depend on what they say.

Store recordings and notes in a folder protected by a password or phone lock. Use codes like 'P1, P2' instead of names in your findings. If you photograph someone's screen, ask first and crop out balances, phone numbers and messages.

Interviews are the most useful research method for a beginner. In 20 to 30 minutes of one-to-one conversation you learn how people really do a task today, what gets in their way, and what words they use. For a small project, **5 to 8 interviews** with people who match your target users usually reveal the main patterns. When you start hearing the same stories again and again, you have enough to move forward.
Two people sitting across from each other having a conversation
A good interview feels like a relaxed conversation guided by your prepared questions.
Ask about the past, not the future

People are poor at predicting what they will do, but good at describing what they did. 'Would you use an app to book fittings?' gets a polite yes. 'Tell me about the last time you booked a fitting' gets the truth: she called three times, the tailor did not pick up, she went in person and waited an hour. Ask **open questions** that start with what, how, tell me about, walk me through. Avoid **leading questions** that suggest an answer.

Ask instead (open)

Would you like a reminder feature?
How do you remember your appointments now?
Is the price too high?

Structure of an interview guide
**Warm-up (2 to 3 minutes):** consent script, simple questions about her day or work.
**Context (5 minutes):** how she currently handles the task, which tools, how often.
**Deep dive (10 to 15 minutes):** the last time she did the task, step by step. Ask 'What happened next?' and 'How did that feel?'
**Pain points (5 minutes):** 'What is the most annoying part?' 'What have you tried to make it easier?'
**Wrap-up (2 minutes):** 'Is there anything I should have asked?' Thank her.
Listen more than you talk

Silence is useful. After she answers, wait a few seconds before your next question. People often add the most honest detail when they fill the pause. Follow up with 'Why was that?' or 'Can you show me?'
From notes to themes: affinity mapping

After the interviews, write each separate observation or quote on its own sticky note or small piece of paper: one idea per note. Spread them out and group notes that are about the same thing. Name each group with a short theme, such as 'Unsure if payment worked' or 'Prefers voice notes to typing'. This is called **affinity mapping** or affinity diagramming. Count how many participants mention each theme. A theme mentioned by 5 out of 6 people matters more than one mentioned once.
Worked example: interviews for a salon booking flow
For example, Blessing is redesigning how customers book appointments at a hair salon in Ikeja that currently takes bookings only by WhatsApp chat. She interviews 6 customers (P1 to P6).
She writes 47 notes from the 6 interviews and groups them into 5 themes.
Theme 1, 'Waiting for a reply': 5 of 6 said they wait hours for the salon to confirm a slot on WhatsApp.
Theme 2, 'Price surprise': 4 of 6 said they learned the full price for braids only at the salon.
Theme 3, 'Wants to see the stylist's work first': 3 of 6 asked friends for photos.
Themes 4 and 5 were mentioned by only 1 or 2 people, so she notes them but does not prioritise them.
She concludes that instant slot confirmation and clear prices are the two biggest needs.
Instead of guessing, Blessing now has evidence: the booking design must show available times and prices up front. Five of six users told her so.
Building a persona

A **persona** summarises a group of similar users as one realistic person, so the team can ask 'Would this work for her?' A good persona is based on your themes. Include: a name and photo placeholder, age range, location and device, goals related to your task, frustrations (pain points), current tools and habits, and one or two real quotes from interviews. Keep it to one page. Avoid stereotypes and irrelevant details such as favourite colour unless your research showed they matter.

A journey map is a timeline from left to right. Across the top you list the **stages** of the experience. Under each stage you add rows: what she **does**, what she **thinks**, how she **feels** (often drawn as a line going up and down), and the **pain points** and **opportunities**. Information architecture and card sorting

**Information architecture (IA)** is the structure behind menus and navigation. Good IA uses the words your users use and groups things the way they expect. A simple way to learn their mental model is **card sorting**: write each content item on a card (for example 'Braids prices', 'Book appointment', 'Stylist photos', 'Opening hours', 'Cancel booking'), then ask 5 or more users to group the cards and name each group. In an **open** card sort users create their own group names; in a **closed** sort you give them the categories. Where most people put a card tells you where to place it in your menu.
Use their words, not yours

If users call it 'hairstyles' and the business calls it 'services', the menu should say 'Hairstyles'. Labels that match the real world are one of Nielsen's heuristics, which you will study in Module 3.
User flows

A **user flow** shows each screen (drawn as a rectangle), each decision (a diamond), and the arrows between them, for one task from start to finish. It forces you to think about what happens when things go wrong: the chosen slot is already taken, the payment fails, the network drops. Draw the 'happy path' first, then add the error paths.
Worked example: flow for 'Book a braiding appointment'
For example, Blessing turns her salon research into a user flow before drawing any screens.
Entry: customer taps a booking link shared on the salon's WhatsApp status.
Screen 1, Choose style: list of hairstyles with photos and starting prices.
Screen 2, Choose date and time: only free slots shown.
Decision: is the slot still free when she taps Confirm? If no, show 'Sorry, that time was just taken' and return to Screen 2 with her style kept.
Screen 3, Details: name and phone number only, two fields.
Screen 4, Pay deposit: through a payment provider such as Paystack, with a clear amount.
Decision: payment successful? If no, show the reason and a 'Try again' button without losing her booking. If yes, go to Screen 5.
Screen 5, Confirmation: date, time, stylist, amount paid, reference number, and 'Add to calendar'.
The flow has 5 screens and 2 decision points, and every pain point from the journey map now has a matching design answer: prices shown, live slots, confirmation with reference.

The happy path should be short; error paths branch off it and return the user without losing her progress.

Before you move on, check your flow against the journey map. Every pain point you chose to fix should have a clear answer somewhere in the flow. If a pain point has no answer, either add a step or decide openly that you will not solve it in this version. Also check the entry point: how does she arrive? A link in a WhatsApp status, a QR code on the salon mirror and a Google Maps listing are all different starting points, and each may need a slightly different first screen.
Keep the number of steps as small as possible, and ask only for information you truly need. Every extra field is a chance for her to give up, especially on a small phone with a slow connection.

Start on paper

Fold an A4 sheet into 4 or 8 parts and sketch a different version of the same screen in each part. This technique, often called **Crazy 8s**, gives you eight quick ideas in about eight minutes. Pick the best parts of each and sketch one clean version of every screen in your user flow.

Building wireframes in Figma
Create a new design file. Press **F** (or **A**) for the Frame tool and choose a phone preset from the right panel, such as an Android or iPhone size.
Use **R** for rectangles (image placeholders, buttons, input fields) and **T** for text. Write real labels, such as 'Book appointment', not 'Button'.
Keep everything in shades of grey. Make the most important action the darkest, largest element on the screen.
Select a group of items and press **Shift + A** to add Auto layout, which keeps spacing even when text changes.
Duplicate the frame for each screen in your user flow and name each frame clearly, for example '02 Choose time'.
Mobile layout rules that matter
**Visual hierarchy:** one main action per screen, placed where the eye lands. Size, weight and position show what matters most.
**Thumb reach:** most people hold the phone in one hand. Put the main button in the lower half of the screen where the thumb reaches easily.
**Touch targets:** Apple's guidelines recommend at least 44 by 44 points and Google's Material Design at least 48 by 48 dp for tappable items. Small links next to each other cause mis-taps.
**Consistent spacing:** many designers use multiples of 8 pixels (8, 16, 24, 32) so screens feel orderly.
**Readable text:** body text large enough to read without zooming, with short lines and plain words.
Making it clickable

In Figma, switch to the **Prototype** tab in the right panel. Select a button, drag the small circle that appears onto the screen it should open, and choose 'On tap' and 'Navigate to'. Repeat for each step in the flow, including a 'Back' link. Press the **Present** (play) button to try it. Use **Share** to copy a link, which participants can open in a browser or the Figma mobile app.

Before you test with users, you can catch many problems yourself by reviewing the design against proven rules of thumb. The best known are **Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics**, first published in 1994 and still used by design teams worldwide. A review against them is called a **heuristic evaluation**. It is quick and cheap, but it does not replace testing with real users; it finds different problems.

Example you may know

Always tell users what is happening, quickly

3. User control and freedom
Provide clear exits and undo
A 'Cancel' button before final payment confirmation
4. Consistency and standards
Same words and patterns everywhere; follow platform norms
The back arrow always in the same place on every screen

Stop mistakes before they happen
Showing the recipient's account name before you confirm a transfer

Show options instead of making users remember
A list of recent beneficiaries instead of retyping account numbers

How to run a heuristic review
Choose the task to review, for example 'book an appointment' in your prototype.
Go through the task screen by screen at least twice: once to understand the flow, once to look for problems.
For each problem, write: the screen, what is wrong, which heuristic it breaks, and a suggested fix.
Give each problem a severity rating from 0 to 4 (see below).
If possible, ask 2 or 3 other people to review separately, then combine lists. Different reviewers find different problems.
Severity ratings
Nielsen suggests rating each problem so the team fixes the worst first. Severity depends on how often it happens, how much it hurts the user when it does, and whether users can get around it.
**0:** not a usability problem.
**1:** cosmetic only; fix if there is time.
**2:** minor; low priority.
**3:** major; important to fix, high priority.
**4:** usability catastrophe; must fix before release.
Worked example: reviewing a school fees payment page
For example, Ngozi reviews a private school's online fees page used by parents in Port Harcourt.
Problem 1: after tapping 'Pay', the page shows a blank white screen for up to 30 seconds. Breaks heuristic 1 (visibility of system status). Parents might pay twice. Severity 4.
Problem 2: the student ID field accepts any text and only shows 'Invalid input' after payment fails. Breaks heuristics 5 and 9. Severity 3.
Problem 3: the menu says 'Remittance' for payments and 'Ledger' for receipts. Breaks heuristic 2. Severity 2.
Problem 4: two different button colours are used for the same 'Next' action. Breaks heuristic 4. Severity 1.
She sorts by severity and recommends fixing problems 1 and 2 before the next term's payments open.
Four problems found in under an hour, ranked so the school knows exactly what to fix first and why.
Fix order by severity
4 Catastrophe: fix now
3 Major: fix soon
2 Minor: plan it
1 Cosmetic: if time
Spend your limited time on the problems that cause the most harm to users first.

Designing for yourself instead of your persona.
Too many choices on one screen, so nothing stands out.
Icons without text labels, which many users cannot interpret.
Error messages that blame the user ('Wrong input!') instead of explaining the fix.
No confirmation for actions that cost money or delete data.
Forgetting what happens when the network fails halfway through a task.

Heuristic reviews have limits. You already know how your design is meant to work, so you will miss problems that confuse a first-time user. You may also judge something as a problem that real users handle easily. That is why the next step in this module is testing with real people. Use the review to clean up the obvious issues first, so your test participants spend their time revealing the problems you could not see.

**Accessibility** means people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate and use your product. This includes people who are blind or have low vision, are deaf or hard of hearing, have limited hand movement, or have cognitive or learning disabilities. It also helps everyone else: an older aunt with weaker eyesight, a mother holding a baby in one arm, someone in bright sunshine at a bus stop.

The international standard is the **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)**, published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). The current version is WCAG 2.2. Its success criteria have levels A, AA and AAA; most organisations aim for **level AA**. WCAG is organised under four principles, often remembered as **POUR**.
WCAG principles (POUR)
Perceivable: can sense it
Operable: can use controls
Understandable: clear and predictable
Robust: works with assistive tech
Every accessibility check you do fits under one of these four principles.

Designing for real Nigerian users
**Low literacy:** use short, common words, pair icons with text labels, and consider voice notes or audio help, which many people already use on WhatsApp.
**Languages:** if your users prefer Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo or Yoruba, test whether key labels should be translated. Never assume English alone is enough.
**Low data and older phones:** compress images, avoid auto-playing video, and make sure the core task works on a small, older Android screen.
**Shared phones:** some users share a phone with family. Do not show sensitive information on the lock screen, and make logging out easy.
**Screen readers:** blind users often use TalkBack on Android or VoiceOver on iPhone. Buttons need real names, so the reader says 'Pay now' instead of 'Button'.
Ethics: no deceptive design

**Deceptive patterns** (also called dark patterns, a term coined by designer Harry Brignull) are design tricks that push people into choices they did not intend. Examples include hidden costs that appear only at the last step, pre-ticked boxes that sign people up for things, 'confirmshaming' buttons such as 'No thanks, I don't want to save money', and making cancellation much harder than sign-up. They may raise short-term numbers but destroy trust, and some may break consumer or data protection rules.
Worked example: making a loan app screen honest and accessible
For example, Aisha is asked to review the sign-up screen of a small savings and loan app aimed at market traders.
She finds light grey text on white. A contrast checker shows about 2.3:1, below the 4.5:1 minimum, so she darkens it.
Form fields use placeholder text only ('Enter phone') that vanishes when typing. She adds visible labels above each field.
A box saying 'Allow access to my contacts' is pre-ticked. She unticks it and adds a plain explanation of why the app asks and that saying no is fine.
Interest and fees appear only after the user accepts. She moves the total repayment amount onto the screen before acceptance.
The error for a wrong phone number is only a red outline. She adds the text 'Phone number should have 11 digits, for example 0803 123 4567'.
Five changes make the screen readable, clear and honest. Users can make an informed choice, which also protects the business's reputation.

Inclusive design is also about who you include in research. If every participant is a young, confident smartphone user in Lagos, your design may fail an older trader in Kano or a first-time smartphone owner in a rural area. Plan your participants so that the people most likely to struggle are part of every round of testing. Their feedback usually improves the product for everyone.
Ask only for data you need

Under Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, personal data should be collected for a clear purpose and kept secure. In design terms: ask for the minimum, explain why you ask, make permissions optional where possible, and never hide consent inside long terms.

A **usability test** means watching real users try to complete real tasks with your design. You do not ask them what they think of it; you observe what they do. It is the single most valuable UX method, because it shows where the design fails in ways that neither you nor a heuristic review would predict.
Why five users?

In a well-known NN/g article, Jakob Nielsen showed that testing with about **5 users** reveals roughly 85 percent of the usability problems in a design, for qualitative testing. After that, each extra user mostly shows you problems you have already seen. His advice is to run several small rounds: test with 5, fix the problems, then test again with another 5. This finds more problems overall than one big test with 15 people.

Planning the test

Write 3 to 5 **task scenarios** that match real goals. Give context without telling them which button to press: 'You want knotless braids this Saturday morning. Book a time.' Not: 'Tap Book, then tap Saturday.'

Prepare your prototype link and a note sheet with one column per task.

During the session

Ask the participant to **think aloud**: say what they are looking at, thinking and trying to do. Your job is to watch and listen. If they ask 'What should I press?', reply 'What would you do if I were not here?' Do not explain the design or rescue them too quickly. Note where they hesitate, what they tap, what they say, and whether they succeed. If you can, ask a colleague to take notes while you guide.

The **System Usability Scale (SUS)**, created by John Brooke, is a standard 10-statement questionnaire answered on a 5-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. The answers convert to a score from 0 to 100. It is not a percentage. Research by Jeff Sauro suggests an average score is around 68, so scores above that are better than average. With only 5 users, treat SUS as a rough signal, not proof.

Worked example: before and after one round of fixes
For example, Blessing tests her salon booking prototype with 5 customers, fixes the worst problems, then tests a new version with 5 different customers.
Round 1: 3 of 5 completed the booking without help (60%). Average time for those 3: 95 seconds. 11 errors in total.
Top problem: 4 of 5 did not notice the deposit amount until the payment screen. Severity 3.
She adds the deposit amount to the style selection screen and makes the 'Confirm' button larger and lower on the screen.
Round 2: 5 of 5 completed without help (100%). Average time: 48 seconds. 3 errors in total.
Average SUS rose from 58 in round 1 to 77 in round 2.
Success went from 60% to 100% and time roughly halved. These before-and-after numbers become strong evidence in her final report and portfolio.
Writing the findings report

Keep it short enough to read in five minutes: what you tested and with whom (codes, not names), the tasks, the key numbers, the top 3 to 5 problems with severity, a screenshot or quote for each, and your recommended fixes. Lead with the most serious problems. Include at least one thing that worked well, so the team knows what to keep.

Remote testing works well when meeting in person is hard. Share the prototype link on WhatsApp, start a video call, and ask the participant to share her screen if her phone allows it, or to describe aloud what she sees and taps. Expect some sessions to drop because of network problems, so book one extra participant per round. Always repeat your consent script at the start of a remote session.
Do not over-claim
Five users show you problems; they do not prove percentages for a whole population. Write '4 of 5 participants' rather than '80% of users', and avoid big claims from small samples.

From wireframe to visual prototype

Only now, after the structure has been tested, should you add visual design. Keep it simple and consistent. You are not trying to win an art prize; you are making the tested design clear and pleasant.

**Choose a small colour palette:** one main colour for primary buttons, one accent, neutral greys for text and backgrounds, plus a red for errors and green for success. Check contrast for every text colour.
**Choose one font family** with two or three sizes: a heading size, a body size and a small size. Many designers use a free Google Font such as Inter or Roboto.
**Make components:** design a button once, select it and choose 'Create component' in Figma. Reuse instances everywhere. When you change the main component, every copy updates.
**Save styles:** save your colours and text sizes as styles or variables so you pick from a set list instead of guessing.
**Replace placeholders** with realistic content: real hairstyle names, real-looking prices marked as examples, and fake but realistic phone numbers.

Worked example: one project, three openings
For example, Blessing prepares three versions of the first paragraph of her salon booking case study.

For a design agency job: 'I led research and design for a salon booking flow. Six interviews revealed that unclear prices and slow WhatsApp replies were the main pain points. After two rounds of testing, task success rose from 3 of 5 to 5 of 5 participants.'

For the salon owner: 'Customers told us they wait hours for replies and are surprised by prices. In testing, the new booking page cut booking time from about 95 seconds to about 48 seconds, and every tester booked without help.'
For a women's business network: 'This simple booking page helps small salon owners take bookings while they work, and was tested with older customers and first-time smartphone users.'
Each version uses the same evidence but leads with what that reader values.
The facts never change; only the order and emphasis change. This keeps her honest while making the work relevant to each audience.
Be honest about results

Use the exact numbers from your tests and say how many participants were involved. Say what you did not test. If your project was a practice project and not launched, say so clearly: 'concept project, tested with 8 participants'. Employers respect honesty and will ask about it in interviews. Never present someone else's design as your own, and if your work was for a client, ask before showing it publicly.
Protect confidential work
If a client or employer asked you to keep their work private, do not post it. You can describe your process in general terms or recreate a similar example with changed details.
Presenting live

Sometimes you will present in person or on a video call. Keep slides few and visual: one slide for the problem, one for what you learned from users, two or three for the design and its changes, one for results and one for next steps. Show the prototype live if the connection is reliable, but keep screenshots ready in case the network fails. End by asking a clear question, such as 'Which of these fixes should we build first?', so the meeting leads to a decision.

Expect questions such as 'How did you choose participants?', 'What would you do with more time?' and 'What did you get wrong?'. Prepare short, honest answers. Saying 'In round one, my price layout confused four of five people, so I changed it' shows strength, not weakness.

You can share a case study as a PDF, on a free portfolio site such as Behance, on a simple personal website, or as a LinkedIn post with images. Keep images light so the page loads on mobile data. Put your best one or two projects first; two strong case studies are better than six weak ones. Add a short line about yourself and how to contact you at the end of each case study.

Why this matters
UX is the whole experience
UX: everything she feels and does with a product
UI: the part you see and touch
Good UX cuts losses, support calls and fear
Works for apps, websites, USSD and paper forms
User experience, or UX, is everything a person feels and does while using a product, from finding it to deciding whether to come back.
User interface, or UI, is only the part you can see and touch: buttons, colours, fonts and screens.
A beautiful screen can still give a bad experience if the button you need is hidden or the words are confusing.
A UX designer studies real users, finds where they struggle, and shapes the product so the task becomes easy, quick and safe.
And it is not only for big companies. A WhatsApp catalogue, a church registration form or a school fees page all have a user experience.
Learn these words
The five components of usability
Learnability: easy on day one?
Efficiency: how fast once she knows it?
Memorability: can she still use it after weeks away?
Errors: how many, how serious, how easy to fix?
Satisfaction: calm or anxious while using it?
Usability has five parts, and you will use these words for the rest of the course.
Learnability. Can a new user send money on a wallet app on day one without help?
Efficiency. Once she knows the app, does buying airtime take 4 taps or 12?
Memorability. Can she find the bill payment menu again after a month away?
Errors. Does the app warn her before sending to the wrong account number?
Satisfaction. Does she feel calm or anxious while the transfer is processing?
Remember too: a product must be usable and also useful. It has to do something she really needs.
Worked example
The transfer that went quiet
For example, Amaka in Onitsha sends money to her supplier on a weak network.
First transfer
Second try, same supplier
Naira amounts are approximate.
Here is a real problem. Amaka in Onitsha sends money to her supplier with a mobile banking app.
After her PIN, the screen spins for about 40 seconds, then returns home with no message at all.
Her first transfer is 25,000 naira. She checks her balance, but the debit has not shown yet.
So she tries again. Both transfers go through.
She has sent 50,000 naira instead of 25,000.
The fix is not a new colour. Show a clear processing, do not retry message, a transaction reference, and a warning about repeat transfers.
The process
Design thinking in five stages
Write problem statements about users, not features.
Empathise: observe and interview real users
Define: write a clear problem statement
Ideate: list many ideas before choosing
Prototype: build a cheap, quick version
Test: watch real users try it, then improve
Designers follow a process so decisions come from evidence, not personal taste. It is called design thinking.
First, empathise. For example, Funke phones 6 members of her learning network who cannot find their certificates.
Second, define. She writes: members cannot find their certificate because it sits under Settings, which they do not link with achievements.
This is the rule. A weak statement says, we need a new menu. A strong one says which user struggles, with what task, and why.
Third, ideate. She asks, how might we help members find their certificate in under 30 seconds? Then she lists 8 ideas before judging any.
Fourth, prototype. She sketches two options on paper.
Fifth, test. She shows them to 5 members and times each one.
The process is a loop. Testing often sends you back to define the problem more sharply, and that is normal.
Research ethics
Three rules to protect people
Explain the purpose, the time, what you record, and that she can stop at any time.
Use codes like P1, P2 instead of names. Keep notes locked and delete them when done.
No PINs, passwords, BVN or account numbers, even in a test. Use fake data instead.
When you interview people, you collect personal information, so treat it with care.
Always get informed consent. She must understand what you are doing, why, how long it takes, what you will record, and that she can stop at any time.
Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for personal data. Follow the basic principles: collect only what you need, keep it safe, and delete it when you are done.
Never ask for bank PINs, passwords, BVN or account numbers, even in a test prototype.
Meet people in public or familiar places, or by phone, and tell someone where you are going.
Every session
For example, Zainab tells a tailor in Kaduna that the interview takes about 20 minutes, and that she is testing ideas, not testing her.
Check these five things before every session. Purpose explained. Time stated. Permission to record. Right to stop. And names removed from your notes.

In this module you learn to find what is wrong before real users suffer it.
First, a quick expert review against Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics, which are rules of thumb.
Second, checks so people with weaker eyesight, less schooling or older phones can use it, and so nothing tricks them.
Third, the most valuable method of all: watching real users try real tasks, and measuring what happens.
Rules of thumb
Five heuristics you will use often
Show status: Processing, then Successful
Use her words: Buy airtime, not VTU top-up
Give exits: Cancel before final payment
Prevent errors: show the account name first
Plain errors that say what to do next
Here are five of the ten. Visibility of system status: always tell her what is happening, quickly.
Match the real world. Say buy airtime, not purchase VTU top-up.
User control. Give a clear cancel button before the final payment.
Error prevention. Show the recipient's account name before she confirms a transfer.
And help her recover. For example: network is slow, your money has not left your account, try again.

Running a heuristic review
Fix severity 4 and 3 problems first.
Choose one task to review
Go through it screen by screen, twice
Note screen, problem, heuristic, fix

Choose one task, then go through it twice: once to understand the flow, once to hunt for problems.

For example, Ngozi reviews a school fees page used by parents in Port Harcourt. After tapping pay, the screen stays blank for up to 30 seconds. That breaks visibility of system status, and parents might pay twice.
She rates it 4, a catastrophe. A confusing menu word gets 2. Two colours for one Next button gets 1.
She recommends fixing the worst problems before the next term's payments open.
Different reviewers find different problems, so combine lists. But a review never replaces testing with real users.

Unticked, with a plain reason
Total repayment shown first
For example, Aisha reviews the sign-up screen of a savings and loan app for market traders.
The grey text is hard to read. The labels vanish when you type. Contacts access is pre-ticked, and interest and fees appear only after the user accepts.
She darkens the text to pass the 4.5 to 1 contrast minimum, adds visible labels, unticks the box and explains why the app asks.
Most important for money, she shows the total repayment before acceptance. Hidden costs and pre-ticked boxes are deceptive patterns. They destroy trust.
Real users
Design for the women who use it
Short common words, icons with text labels, and voice help like WhatsApp voice notes.
Test whether key labels need Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo or Yoruba. English alone may not be enough.
Small images, no auto-play video, nothing sensitive on the lock screen, easy log out.
Accessibility helps everyone: an older aunt, a mother holding a baby, someone in bright sunshine. Pair every icon with a word.
Never assume English alone is enough. Test your key labels.
Many users share a phone and pay for data. Make the core task work on a small, older Android screen, and ask only for the data you truly need.
Blessing's two test rounds
Round 1
3 of 5 succeeded alone
95 seconds on average
11 errors
SUS score 58
Round 2
5 of 5 succeeded alone
48 seconds on average
3 errors
SUS score 77
Testing with about 5 users shows most of the problems. Blessing gives 5 customers a real scenario and asks them to think aloud. Only 3 of 5 book without help, and 4 of 5 miss the deposit amount.
She shows the deposit earlier and makes Confirm larger, then tests 5 new customers. All 5 succeed, the time roughly halves, and the System Usability Scale score rises from 58 to 77.
How to run a fair test
Repeat your consent script
Give a goal, not button instructions
Ask her to think aloud
Do not explain or rescue too quickly
Note hesitations, taps, words, success
Say, you want braids this Saturday morning, book a time. Never say, tap Book.
If she asks what to press, reply: what would you do if I were not here? And write 4 of 5 participants, never 80 percent of users. Small tests show problems, not proof.
Key points
Remember
Review with the 10 heuristics; rate severity 0 to 4
Contrast 4.5:1, visible labels, never colour alone
No hidden costs or pre-ticked boxes
Test with 5, fix the worst, test again
Measure success, time, errors and SUS
To remember. Review first and fix the worst problems. Make it readable and honest. Then test with 5 users, fix, and test again, measuring success, time, errors and SUS.

Blessing's final quality check

Tell the story
The five parts of a case study
Keep the facts the same. Change only what you lead with.
The problem and the users
Your role and your limits
Research and the top themes
Design, and what changed after testing
Results and what you would do next
Employers look for how you think, not just finished screens. Start with who struggled with what, then say what you did yourself and your limits, such as budget, devices or data.
Share your top 2 or 3 themes with a short quote. Then show one before and after, because side-by-side comparisons backed by test numbers convince people most.
End with your real numbers and an honest reflection.
You will tailor the opening for each reader, but the evidence never changes.
Know your reader
One project, three openings
Lead with process: six interviews, two test rounds, success up from 3 of 5 to 5 of 5.
Lead with business: booking time cut from about 95 to about 48 seconds.
Lead with who is helped: tested with older customers and first-time smartphone users.
Blessing writes three openings. For a design agency job, she leads with her research methods and her iterations.
For the salon owner, she leads with customers: shorter booking time, and every tester booked without help.
For a women's business network, she leads with inclusion and who benefits.
Be honest
Honest results build trust
Do
Exact numbers and participant counts
Say what you did not test
Say concept project if not launched
Present someone else's design
Post work a client kept private
Big claims from tiny samples
Use your exact test numbers and say how many people took part. A practice project can say, concept project, tested with 8 participants. Employers respect that.
Never show someone else's work as yours, and ask a client before showing their work publicly.
Saying, my price layout confused four of five people, so I changed it, shows strength, not weakness.
Halima's 90-day plan
Written scope first. Deposit through a traceable channel.
Days 1 to 30: a second tested case study
Days 31 to 60: one real business and a testimonial
Days 61 to 90: first paid project with a scope
Every Friday: a 15-minute review
For example, Halima is a mother of two in Abuja with about 6 hours a week. She splits 90 days into three 30-day blocks, each with one goal and a number to check.
First, a second project tested with 5 users.
Next, she offers a low-cost heuristic review to 2 local businesses each week, until one agrees and gives a written testimonial.
Then her first paid project. Beware offers that ask you to pay for a guaranteed job. Real clients agree a written scope first, and Halima takes a deposit by bank transfer or a Paystack payment link.
Every Friday she spends 15 minutes ticking off actions. Plan for the hours you really have, not the hours you wish you had.
